current_description.description_long: In June 2019, Manhattan prosecutors were preparing to prosecute Paul Manafort on New York state charges while he was serving a federal sentence. NBC News, citing contemporaneous reporting and officials, said Manafort’s lawyer asked the Bureau of Prisons to keep him in federal custody because of concerns about his health and safety at Rikers Island. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen then contacted Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance’s office, attached the lawyer’s letter, and asked for its response. Vance’s office said it had not proposed housing Manafort at Rikers and took no position on whether he should remain in federal custody. Federal officials ultimately kept Manafort in federal custody at the Metropolitan Correctional Center while making him available to state prosecutors. The available accounts support DOJ involvement in the placement decision after a defense request, but not the original claim that DOJ independently ordered Manafort kept out of Rikers. The record also does not establish political direction from Trump.
current_description.description_medium: NBC News reported in June 2019 that Paul Manafort’s lawyer asked federal officials to keep him in federal custody, citing health and safety concerns about Rikers Island. proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump Pressures Postmaster DeJoy to Slow Mail Delivery Before 2020 Election
proposal.original_synopsis: In mid-2020, Postmaster General Louis DeJoy, a major Trump donor with no postal experience, implemented operational changes to the U.S. Postal Service that slowed mail delivery across the country. The changes included eliminating overtime, removing mail sorting machines, and reducing delivery trips — all in the lead-up to a historic mail-in ballot election during the COVID-19 pandemic. Congressional Democrats and election officials accused the changes of being deliberate voter suppression to benefit Trump. DeJoy was forced to pause some changes under court order. Trump explicitly stated he was opposing postal funding because he didn't want to make it easier for mail-in voting, directly linking postal sabotage to election strategy.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends CDC Funding for Abortion Research and Contraceptive Access Programs
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration ended all CDC grants and programs related to abortion research, contraceptive access, and reproductive health services. Dozens of federally funded programs that provided contraception counseling, teen pregnancy prevention, and maternal health research were terminated. Researchers studying maternal mortality — which is significantly higher in the United States than in other wealthy countries — had their grants cancelled mid-study. The cuts disproportionately impacted low-income women and those in rural areas with limited access to private healthcare. Reproductive health advocates noted that eliminating contraceptive access programs would likely increase unintended pregnancies and abortions, directly contradicting the stated anti-abortion goals of the administration.

identified_problems.explanation: No April 2025 executive order matching the described expansion of material-support law was located.

A January 29 antisemitism order directed agencies to use existing civil and criminal authorities, and DOJ later announced a terrorism-law investigation connected to Columbia protests. Those are distinct actions and do not establish a new executive-order definition criminalizing criticism, donations or association as described.

frozen_original.title: Trump executive order allowing prosecution of critics for material support of terrorism
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump signed an executive order that could allow the prosecution of domestic critics and activists under material support for terrorism statutes, effectively criminalizing political dissent. The order broadly expanded the definition of material support to potentially include speech, donations, and association with organizations designated as terrorist-adjacent by the administration. Civil liberties advocates warned the order could be used to prosecute anyone who donated to or participated in protests organized by groups the administration had targeted.
